https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, President Trump and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Oval Office By Tom Bateman State department correspondent Published 18 September 2026, 01:42 BST Updated 02:31 BST President Donald Trump's administration says it has approved the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a policy shift for the US that has raised concerns from some members of Congress. Saudi Arabia has sought for years to buy the world's most advanced warplane, equipped with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection. Washington had resisted, partly because it supplies F-35s to its ally Israel, which is guaranteed under US law to receive top-of-the-range American weapons compared with those its regional neighbours can access. Congress has 30 days to scrutinise or attempt to block the $24bn (Â£17.8bn) sale to Riyadh, which is the largest customer for US weapons. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, A US Air Force F-35 Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday. He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party". Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia. They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries. The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives". It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region". "The proposed â sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military â balance in the region," the state department added. Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November. The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed â described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history". The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin. This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets. However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May , external that it would procure another F-35 squadron. This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post , external . Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m. Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018. Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its â relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered. The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen. The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces. The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/19/on-b.text: While irregular migration is declining along several routes into the European Union, the opposite is happening on Crete. The Greek island, better known for its beaches and tourism industry, is facing a sharp increase in arrivals from North Africa and Asia.Around 24,000 migrants reached Crete during the first ten months of 2026, compared with approximately 17,000 throughout 2025.Most boats depart from eastern Libya, crossing hundreds of kilometres of open sea towards Gavdos, a small island south of Crete, or the southern coastline of Crete itself.Despite increased patrols, surveillance aircraft and sophisticated monitoring technology, the crossings continue.To understand what is happening on Europe's southern maritime frontier, Euronews joined a patrol of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, Frontex, spending time with its crews at sea and visiting the facilities coordinating aerial surveillance.A search for missing migrantsDuring our reporting, an incident illustrated the dangers of this increasingly busy migration route.On the afternoon of November 4, a migrant was discovered alone on Chrissi Island, approximately 15 kilometres off Crete’s southern coast.He claimed to have travelled with 60 other people, triggering an extensive search and rescue operation.It is just one of dozens of incidents requiring a response from Greek and European patrol and rescue teams operating off Crete.Local Coast Guard officials in Heraklion told Euronews that, in just 48 hours, 13 boats carrying approximately 400 migrants had arrived within their area of responsibility. During the same period, around 20 migrants were also found dead- a stark reminder of the human cost of the increasingly dangerous crossing to Europe's southern shores.A Latvian ship guarding Europe's bordersGreece hosts Frontex's largest operational presence in the European Union, with the agency supporting Greek authorities across a wide range of activities.The agency provides technical equipment, surveillance capabilities and support for return operations involving migrants who have no legal right to remain in the EU. All these activities are carried out in cooperation with the Greek authorities, who retain operational command.In Crete and Gavdos -the small Greek island south of Crete and the southernmost inhabited island in Europe- alone, more than 40 officers, three aircraft, an unmanned aircraft and six patrol vessels have been deployed to support Greek authorities.Among them is Valpas, a Latvian patrol vessel operating south of Crete for approximately 18 months. A typical patrol aboard Valpas lasts 72 hours. For its 20-member crew, the ship becomes both a workplace and a temporary home.Leaving their families behind, crew members try to maintain a connection with Latvia, keeping familiar traditions alive even while operating far from home. Captain Ozers, a father of three, speaks to his children every evening.Captain Ozers told Euronews that rescue operations can be extremely difficult and dangerous, both for the migrants attempting the crossing and for the crews trying to bring them to safety.He recalled one of the most challenging moments he has faced at sea:“Sometimes, everyone tries to stand up at once, which can cause the boat to capsize. I experienced this myself during an operation when two people fell overboard. We were fortunate that only two ended up in the water. It was nighttime, but we managed to keep them in sight throughout. We threw them lifebuoys and other flotation devices while we first secured the larger group of passengers on the boat. Once they were safe, we moved away from the boat and manoeuvred closer to the two people in the water.”Weather conditions make these operations even more challenging. Captain Ozers explained that one of the greatest dangers arises when migrants set off in favourable weather, only to face deteriorating conditions during their journey.“The most difficult for us is when they start their voyage with the nice weather and then the weather becomes bad. We need to plan how to pick them up and it becomes a little bit dangerous.”Ioannis Orphanos, Commander of the Hellenic Coast Guard’s 7th Regional Command, which oversees Coast Guard operations across Crete, explained that rescue operations can be particularly challenging.“Some incidents are extremely difficult, and unfortunately, there are times when lives are lost. We must remember that the area is vast and weather conditions are often adverse. We may be dealing with people who have never experienced the sea before, who are completely unfamiliar with the maritime environment and may not even know how to swim,” he told Euronews.Eyes in the skyFrontex's operations also rely on advanced aerial surveillance. From Tympaki airfield in Crete, Frontex operates the Heron 1, a highly advanced long-endurance surveillance drone equipped with sophisticated radar, high-resolution cameras and thermal imaging technology. It can remain airborne for more than 20 hours, monitoring vast stretches of the Libyan Sea both day and night.Its images are transmitted live to the Hellenic Coast Guard's operations centre in Piraeus and Frontex headquarters in Warsaw, while Greek authorities retain operational command.Evangelos Diamantis, Head of the Monitoring and Surveillance Sector at the Frontex Operation Centre, explained why early detection is crucial:“The boats used by smuggling networks are not seaworthy. They often have faulty engines, which means there is no guarantee they will reach their destination — the European shores, in this case Greece. They are always overcrowded, making them highly vulnerable to sinking or accidents, especially when combined with bad weather. So, detecting these boats early increases the chances of rescuing the people on board and bringing them safely to shore.”Growing tensions on CreteYet increased surveillance has not stopped migrants from reaching the island. Newcomers are transferred directly to four tightly controlled temporary accommodation facilities, where they await transportation to mainland Greece. The continuing arrivals are fuelling increasingly strong opposition among residents and local authorities, who object to migrants remaining in their communities.Crete is therefore facing pressure on two fronts: managing a growing number of arrivals while dealing with mounting local resistance.For the European Union, the challenge extends beyond the Greek island.As migration routes shift and surveillance capabilities expand, a fundamental question remains: how can Frontex become more effective in managing irregular migration while fulfilling its responsibility to protect human lives at sea?
